title: How scarce is expert data work?
question: Are people who can write high-quality expert training data for large models actually scarce?
answer: Scarce. But to command a good price, the proof is not "few people can do this"; it is a before-and-after comparison showing which questions the model got better at because of your data.

reasoning_chain.step: Start from a measurable reference point: Mercor, a platform that matches domain experts with AI labs to write data, has more than 30,000 weekly active contractors.
Scale by population: 30,000 ÷ 8 billion ≈ 4 per million people, a tiny share of the population.

But 30,000 is one company's active headcount, not the total number of capable people. There are millions of STEM master's and PhD holders worldwide, so the real pool is larger than 30,000, yet still a very small share of the population.

Scarcity in a market is about supply and demand, not about share of population. On the demand side, Mercor's annualised revenue passed $2 billion in June 2026, double the start of the year, and it pays contractors about $2 million a day, so buyers are growing fast.
Conclusion: scarce relative to population, and currently undersupplied relative to demand.

Mercor pays contractors roughly 60% to 70% of revenue `[checked]` Same source

common_errors: Saying "there are plenty of them" from the absolute number alone, ignoring the share of population (Claude made this mistake in the conversation and the user corrected it).
Saying "scarce, therefore valuable" from the population share alone, ignoring the size of demand.

title: "Need" versus "effective demand"
question: Is effective demand a pseudo-concept? If people didn't have to pay for things, would it still exist?
answer: Effective demand is a constraint specific to monetary economies, not a pseudo-concept. Remove money-based allocation and the constraint shifts from "do you have money" to "are you entitled"; the problem changes form rather than disappearing.

reasoning_chain.step: Definition: effective demand is demand backed by the ability to pay. Someone who needs bread but has no money does not count in the market.
Premise: money is, at bottom, credit. So "effective demand" describes whose needs the credit system recognises.
So it is not a pseudo-concept; it is a concept that holds only in a monetary exchange economy (the user's own precise formulation).
If allocation does not depend on paying, that constraint does disappear.
But the question "who gets what" does not disappear; it is settled by other rules: rationing, queues, status, connections.
Kornai called the typical pathology of planned economies the "shortage economy": market economies suffer from being unable to sell, planned economies from not having enough to go round.

key_facts.text: Keynes, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936), introduced deficient effective demand `[common]`
Kornai, Economics of Shortage (1980) `[common]`

common_errors: Treating a concept with limited scope as a false concept.
Assuming non-market allocation has no allocation problem.

title: AI services in poorer regions: who pays?
question: In places like Africa and South America, with low purchasing power and weak sovereign credit, how would AI digital workers charge and get paid? Everyone else is doing charity, so why charge at all?
answer: Don't charge the poor; charge the institutions that pay on their behalf. What you charge for is continued operation, maintenance and measurable outcomes.

reasoning_chain.step: Per-capita purchasing power is low, so selling directly to individuals does not work.

Sovereign credit risk is high: Zambia (2020), Ghana (2022) and Ethiopia (2023) have all defaulted, and the Nigerian and Argentine currencies have fallen sharply. Receivables should not depend on local governments.
Who can pay: telecom operators, banks, agribusinesses and cooperatives, international aid agencies and development banks.

Settlement: sign contracts in US dollars or euros, collected by an offshore entity; collect small local fees through mobile wallets (such as M-Pesa or MTN MoMo), priced in dollars and charged in local currency at the day's rate.

Cost: open-weight small models, quantised to run offline on edge devices; answer common questions locally and route hard ones to a large model; fine-tune open-source speech recognition models on local languages.

Why charge: charity projects often die after the pilot, with no one maintaining them once grants stop ("pilot-itis"); aid agencies themselves buy services from vendors; end users can use it free while institutions pay per volume of service or per outcome.

title: Why not move low-end manufacturing to Africa?
question: China, Vietnam and Japan all rose by taking on manufacturing. Why can't Africa?
answer: It can be done, and there are successes, but compared with East Asia back then there is the extra hurdle of automation, and it is capital-heavy, slow and politically risky.

reasoning_chain.step: Start with what has happened: Ethiopia built industrial parks (Hawassa) and attracted garment and footwear factories, then lost many orders after civil war and the 2022 withdrawal of its US AGOA duty-free status. Morocco's car industry succeeded, thanks to proximity to Europe, good ports and stable policy.
Obstacle 1: infrastructure. Unreliable power and expensive inland transport; building your own power plant eats up the cheap-labour advantage.
Obstacle 2: market fragmentation. More than fifty countries, each with its own tariffs, currency and regulations.
Obstacle 3: political stability. One civil war can empty an industrial park.
Obstacle 4: automation reduces the weight of labour costs, which Rodrik calls "premature deindustrialisation".
Obstacle 5: a shortage of a large workforce with basic education, and of supporting supply chains.

Rodrik, "Premature Deindustrialization" (2016) `[common]`

common_errors: Looking only at labour costs and ignoring power, logistics and political risk.

title: The consumption paradox of full automation
question: If everything were automated, why would anyone still need to work? Couldn't the rich just enjoy their wealth?
answer: After automation the question is not "do we still need to work" but "without labour, how is wealth distributed, and where do people find meaning".

reasoning_chain.step: If the factories belong to one person and nobody else has income, who buys the products?
If nobody buys, the products are worth nothing; money is worth something only because people are willing to exchange labour and goods for it.
So when wealth is concentrated to the extreme, wealth itself loses meaning.
Today labour serves three functions: distribution (wages), order (mass unemployment brings unrest) and meaning (identity and dignity).
If labour is no longer needed, a replacement distribution mechanism is required: universal basic income, broader capital ownership, taxes on automation. Each has supporters and critics.

IMF (2024): about 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, about 60% in advanced economies `[common]`

title: Surplus alongside hunger
question: Lots of bread and milk get thrown away while many people can't afford to eat. Doesn't that show the system is broken?
answer: The failure is a fact; the direction of the remedy is a contested political judgement.

reasoning_chain.step: Historical precedent: in the Great Depression American farmers poured away milk while people in cities queued for relief.
The FAO's long-standing conclusion: global food production is enough to feed everyone; hunger comes mainly from poverty, conflict and distribution.
So "surplus alongside hunger" shows a failure of the distribution mechanism; that much is factually true.
How deep the failure goes and how to fix it divides into three main views:
sub: A structural defect requiring institutional change;
Repair within the market framework (minimum income guarantees, redistribution, broader capital ownership);
The main causes are war, corruption and trade barriers, and markets themselves are the main engine of poverty reduction.

key_facts.text: FAO: hunger is mainly a problem of access, not of production `[common]`

common_errors: Jumping from "there is a failure" straight to "a particular ideology is right".

title: An ethical classification of digital workers
question: Digital workers take people's jobs. Is it still worth building them?
answer: Gap-filling and augmentation are worth doing; pure substitution calls for caution. This is a choice that can be made at the product design stage.

reasoning_chain.step: Classify by what position it fills:
sub: Substitution: takes over work people are already doing, purely to cut costs.
Gap-filling: goes where no one is available (villages without vets, care homes short of carers).
Augmentation: one person does the work of three, with income rising accordingly.

reasoning_chain.step: Technology will not stop because one person declines to build it.
So the key question is not "build or not" but "which category does this particular product fall into".

common_errors: Treating all automation as taking jobs.

title: Welfare states and capital flight
question: Europe built basic social protection, but other countries don't play by the same rules, so firms move to cheaper places. Doesn't that inevitably lead to economic fatigue?
answer: Where capital moves freely and protection can only be delivered within one country, welfare systems are under constant pressure. Whether the answer is to slow globalisation or to build cross-border rules remains contested.

reasoning_chain.step: Premise: if a country's citizens can't afford food, something has gone wrong with its politics and economy, which is why Europe built basic protection (the user's argument).
Protection raises domestic costs.
Capital moves freely; firms relocate to countries with lower costs and fewer rules.
The tax base erodes and the protection system becomes harder to sustain. This is the "race to the bottom".
Rodrik's "globalisation trilemma": deep globalisation, national sovereignty and democratic politics; at most two can be achieved at once.

Existing remedies: the global minimum corporate tax (OECD Pillar Two, 15%), the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, labour and environmental clauses in trade agreements. As long as some countries stay out, loopholes remain.

common_errors: Attributing capital flight only to "economic downturn" or "debt-driven growth", ignoring regulatory arbitrage.

title: The arithmetic of leverage and deleveraging
question: Borrowing lets one dollar act like ten. But when the debt is repaid, how much money disappears from the market?
answer: Deleveraging genuinely shrinks the money supply, and it is self-reinforcing through falling asset prices.

reasoning_chain.step: Own 1, borrow 9, buy assets worth 10: leverage of 10x.
If the assets fall 10%, 9 is left, exactly enough to repay; the equity is wiped out. In general, with leverage L, a fall of 1/L wipes out the equity.
When a bank lends, it records a deposit in the borrower's account, and money is created; when the loan is repaid, that deposit is cancelled and the money disappears.
So when the whole economy deleverages at once, money in circulation really shrinks, by roughly the amount of net repayment.
Selling assets to repay debt pushes asset prices down, wipes out more people's equity, and triggers a chain of forced selling.

key_facts.text: Bank of England, "Money creation in the modern economy" (2014): commercial bank lending creates deposits `[common]`
Fisher, "The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions" (1933) `[common]`

common_errors: Thinking repayment just moves money from one person to another, leaving the total unchanged.

title: The loop of debt, automation and unemployment
question: What shock comes from deleveraging combined with automation and unemployment?
answer: The three form a mutually reinforcing deflationary loop. The usual remedy is for the government to take on leverage, which raises the question of who repays the government's debt.

reasoning_chain.step: Unemployment lowers income, but the nominal amount of debt does not change.
Automation pushes prices down, so the same nominal debt becomes a heavier real burden (Fisher: the more you repay, the more you owe).
Defaults rise, banks tighten lending, money shrinks further, firms hire less, and we are back at step 1.

Richard Koo used "balance sheet recession" to explain Japan's stagnation after the 1990s: the private sector only repaid debt and stopped borrowing, so even zero interest rates could not stimulate it.
Mainstream response: when the private sector deleverages, the government borrows and spends in the opposite direction.

common_errors: Treating all automation-driven price declines as good, ignoring their effect on debtors.

title: Is China like Japan?
question: Is China today essentially the same as Japan back then?
answer: Contested; both judgements have defensible arguments.

One side argues these differences are enough to let China avoid Japanese-style stagnation; the other argues the underlying mechanism is the same (the user's view).

title: The economic background of Japan's 1930s expansion
question: How was Japan's turn to militarism related to debt and to the example set by the British and other empires?
answer: Economic crisis and an imperialist international order are important background, but the expansion cannot be attributed simply to "getting rid of debt". The debt was ultimately eliminated by erasing household savings.

reasoning_chain.step: The Great Depression hit Japan hard: rural bankruptcy, a small domestic market, a need for resources and markets.

International setting: the 1919 Paris Peace Conference rejected Japan's racial equality proposal; the Washington Naval Treaty capped its capital-ship ratio; in 1932 Britain set up imperial preference through the Ottawa Agreements, and the major empires closed their markets.
Latecomers saw earlier powers holding colonies and closed economic blocs and tried to copy the model. This explains the behaviour; it does not justify it.
Domestic politics: the military gradually overpowered civilian government through assassinations and coups.
The war was financed with government bonds and central bank financing; the longer it went on, the larger the debt.
After the war, hyperinflation and a one-off property tax in 1946 wiped out the war debt, at the cost of nearly erasing household savings.
Counterexample: post-war Japan had no colonies and became the world's second-largest economy through open trade.

title: Germany: unpayable debt and desperation
question: What happens if you load a country with debt it can never repay?
answer: Unpayable debt is either renegotiated and reduced, or settled through inflation, upheaval or even war; it does not vanish by being set aside.

reasoning_chain.step: Post-WWI reparations could not be paid off in any foreseeable time; Keynes warned of the consequences in The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919).
Then came hyperinflation, the Great Depression and the Nazis' rise to power.
After WWII the Allies learned the lesson: the 1953 London Debt Agreement substantially reduced West Germany's debt, followed by the economic miracle.
Germany paid the last instalment related to WWI debt in 2010.

title: Debt is arithmetic; the blockage is political
question: Does debt mean the sky is falling?
answer: Mathematically there is always a solution; the real obstacle is that nobody wants to acknowledge and bear the loss.

reasoning_chain.step: Rollover and restructuring: lengthen maturities, lower interest rates (London Debt Agreement, 1953).
Write-downs: cut the principal directly (the 1989 Brady Plan for Latin American debt).
Inflation: reduce the real value of debt (moderate inflation in the UK and US after WWII).
Growth: as long as the economy grows faster than the interest rate, debt as a share of GDP falls on its own.
Japan's government debt exceeds twice GDP yet it functions normally, because creditors are mainly domestic and the central bank cooperates.
Every solution is essentially a decision about who bears the loss: creditors, taxpayers, savers or the next generation.

common_errors: Treating debt as a purely technical problem and ignoring distribution.

title: A way out for personal debt: Shenzhen personal bankruptcy
question: When countries can't repay, they can restructure or inflate. What can an individual do?
answer: Shenzhen has a formal personal bankruptcy route; elsewhere, enforcement proceedings are currently the main mechanism.

reasoning_chain.step: Countries have many debt tools; individuals have far fewer options.
Most of China has no personal bankruptcy system; people who can't repay are listed as dishonest judgement debtors.
Shenzhen is the exception: the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone Personal Bankruptcy Regulations took effect on 1 March 2021, the first in the country.
